generator: claude monthly run (manual, regenerated late month)
intro: Only the last week of November is left, so each deep dive fits about one week. Pick one, two or all three. Skipping is fine.

items.title: Speculative decoding: faster LLMs with the same outputs
items.why: Speculative decoding is now built into most serving stacks. It is also a neat piece of probability: a small model guesses, a big model checks, and the output distribution does not change. Knowing why it is exact helps you judge new inference papers quickly.
items.objective: Prove to yourself that the accept and reject rule keeps the target distribution, measure a real speedup on your own machine, and explain when the trick stops paying off.
prerequisites: basic PyTorch and Hugging Face transformers
expected value of a geometric-like series

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: why the trick is exact
tasks: Read Leviathan, Kalman and Matias: the abstract, the introduction, the algorithm and the analysis of how many tokens are accepted per step
On paper, show that accepting a draft token with probability min(1, p/q) and otherwise sampling from the leftover distribution gives exactly p
Read the Chen et al. abstract and method. Note one way their setup differs from Leviathan et al.

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: measure it and meet the variants
tasks: Follow the Hugging Face assisted decoding guide. Run SmolLM-1.7B with SmolLM-135M as the assistant and time tokens per second against plain decoding
Try prompt lookup decoding with prompt_lookup_num_tokens=5 on a summarisation prompt, where the output copies the input
Write the accept and reject rule from scratch for two toy distributions and check by sampling that the output matches p
Skim the Medusa abstract and the dynamic speculation blog post. Write one line on what each changes about drafting

primary_resource.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
primary_resource.creator: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias
primary_resource.note: ICML 2023. Reports 2x to 3x faster decoding on T5-XXL with identical outputs.

resources.title: Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling
resources.creator: Charlie Chen, Sebastian Borgeaud, Geoffrey Irving, Jean-Baptiste Lespiau, Laurent Sifre, John Jumper
resources.note: The same idea, found independently, on a 70B model.

resources.title: Assisted decoding (Transformers documentation)
resources.creator: Hugging Face
resources.note: Short runnable code for each method.

resources.title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
resources.creator: Tianle Cai, Yuhong Li, Zhengyang Geng, Hongwu Peng, Jason D. Lee, Deming Chen, Tri Dao
resources.note: Drafts with extra heads on the big model instead of a separate small model.

resources.title: Faster Assisted Generation with Dynamic Speculation
resources.creator: Intel Labs and Hugging Face
resources.note: The draft model stops early when it is unsure.

resources.title: Universal Assisted Generation: Faster Decoding with Any Assistant Model
resources.creator: Intel Labs and Hugging Face
resources.note: Optional. How to use a draft model with a different tokenizer.

exercises: If each draft token is accepted with probability a and you draft g tokens, show that the expected number of tokens per big-model call is (1 - a^(g+1)) / (1 - a)
Plot that expression for a = 0.6 and a = 0.9 as g grows. Where does drafting more stop helping?
items.deliverable: A one-page note with the exactness proof in your own words, your measured speedup, and one case where speculative decoding would not help.
items.definition_of_done: You can explain without notes why the output distribution is unchanged and what acceptance rate means for speed.
items.final_synthesis: Write one research question about speculative decoding that matters for your area, such as how it interacts with quantized draft models or with safety filtering.
items.light_version: Read the Leviathan et al. abstract and algorithm, then do only the exactness proof on paper.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: tree-based drafting and serving systems such as vLLM. Not scheduled automatically.

items.title: Statistical mechanics behind softmax, energy and free energy
items.why: Softmax with a temperature, energy-based models, the partition function and the ELBO all come from statistical mechanics. Learning the physics once makes many ML ideas feel like one idea. This is the growth item for the month.
items.objective: Derive the Boltzmann distribution, explain the partition function and free energy, and map each one to its ML twin.

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: the physics
tasks: Read Tong, Statistical Physics, chapter 1: section 1.2.3 The Two State System, then 1.3 The Canonical Ensemble, 1.3.1 The Partition Function and 1.3.4 Free Energy
Optional: read Feynman Lectures Vol. I, chapter 40, The Principles of Statistical Mechanics, for intuition
Derive the Boltzmann distribution by maximising entropy with a fixed mean energy

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: the ML twins
tasks: Read LeCun et al., A Tutorial on Energy-Based Learning: section 1.3 for the Gibbs distribution and partition function, and section 2.2.4 for free energy as a log partition function
Read the Nobel Prize 2024 popular information on Hopfield's energy and the Boltzmann machine
Code a 16-unit Hopfield network that stores two patterns. Start from a noisy pattern and print the energy at each update

primary_resource.title: Statistical Physics, chapter 1: The Fundamentals of Statistical Mechanics
primary_resource.creator: David Tong (University of Cambridge)
primary_resource.note: Free lecture notes, clear and short.

resources.title: A Tutorial on Energy-Based Learning
resources.creator: Yann LeCun, Sumit Chopra, Raia Hadsell, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Fu Jie Huang

resources.title: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2024: popular information
resources.creator: The Nobel Prize
resources.note: How Hopfield networks use an energy and how the Boltzmann machine uses Boltzmann's equation.

resources.title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I
resources.creator: Richard Feynman
resources.chapters: Chapter 40, The Principles of Statistical Mechanics
resources.note: Free to read on the Caltech site. The page could not be fetched this run, so no link.

resources.title: Information Theory, Inference and Learning Algorithms
resources.creator: David J. C. MacKay
resources.chapters: 31 Ising models, 33 Variational methods, 42 Hopfield networks, 43 Boltzmann machines
resources.note: Optional, for going further. Link is the publisher page.

exercises: Show that softmax(z / T) is a Boltzmann distribution with energy -z and temperature T. What happens as T goes to 0 and to infinity?
Show that log Z equals the maximum over q of (-E_q[energy] + H(q)). Then point to where this same step appears in the ELBO
items.deliverable: A one-page dictionary with two columns: physics word and ML word, with one equation per row.
items.definition_of_done: You can explain without notes why the free energy is a log partition function and why that makes the ELBO a bound.
items.final_synthesis: Write one question that physics might answer about learning, such as whether sudden jumps in training look like phase transitions.
items.light_version: Read Tong section 1.3 up to the partition function, then do only the softmax exercise.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: phase transitions in learning, or MacKay's Ising and variational chapters. Not scheduled automatically.

cross_domain.connection: The Boltzmann distribution, partition function and free energy reappear as softmax, normalising constants and the ELBO.

items.title: Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali: a week with one film
items.why: Pather Panchali is one of the great films about ordinary life. A family, a village, rain and a passing train become something you remember for years. Spending a week with one film trains slow attention, the opposite of scrolling.
items.objective: Watch Pather Panchali closely, read two good essays on it, and make one small piece of your own about an everyday sight.
prerequisites: about two hours for the film, with English subtitles

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: watch it fresh
tasks: Watch Pather Panchali (1955, Bengali, 125 minutes) without reading anything first
Right after, write down three moments that stayed with you and one line on why
Read Terrence Rafferty's Criterion essay, Every Common Sight. Compare his moments with yours

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: look again, then make something
tasks: Read Girish Shambu's Criterion essay, Behind the Universal, and rewatch one scene it discusses
Read the RogerEbert.com feature on the restoration of the trilogy
Make your own every common sight: six photos or 150 words about one ordinary thing near you, seen slowly
Optional: watch the next film, Aparajito (1956)

primary_resource.title: Pather Panchali
primary_resource.creator: Satyajit Ray
primary_resource.note: Bengali, black and white, 125 minutes. First film of the Apu Trilogy.

resources.title: The Apu Trilogy: Every Common Sight
resources.creator: Terrence Rafferty (Criterion)

resources.title: The Apu Trilogy: Behind the Universal
resources.creator: Girish Shambu (Criterion)

resources.title: Cinematic Poetry: The Restoration of The Apu Trilogy
resources.creator: RogerEbert.com
resources.note: How the films were saved after a fire, and how the mother holds the story together.

resources.title: Our Films, Their Films
resources.creator: Satyajit Ray
resources.note: Optional. Ray's own essays on making films.

exercises: Pick one scene and count the shots. Where is the camera, high or low, close or far?
Listen to the music alone for a minute. What does it tell you before the picture does?
items.deliverable: Your three moments and your six photos or 150 words.
items.definition_of_done: You have watched the film and can describe one scene in detail to a friend.
items.final_synthesis: Write two sentences: what does Ray make you notice that you usually pass by?
items.light_version: Watch the film and write your three moments. Skip the essays.
items.continuation: Possible later: the rest of the Apu Trilogy, or Ray's Charulata. Not scheduled automatically.

cross_domain.connection: Ray's way of seeing ordinary life is a lesson in framing that carries straight into everyday photography.

plans.goal: Order something politely: get attention, ask for an item, ask the price and say thank you.

weeks.focus: Wed 25 and Thu 26: get attention and ask
tasks: Learn すみません (sumimasen, excuse me) and これをください (kore o kudasai, this one please). Say each out loud ten times
Learn お水をください (omizu o kudasai, water please)
Listen to NHK Easy Japanese lesson 45 and shadow the request

weeks.focus: Sat 28 and Sun 29: price and thanks
tasks: Learn いくらですか (ikura desu ka, how much is it?) and ありがとうございます (arigatō gozaimasu, thank you very much)
Role-play ordering at a café with Claude, twice
Say the full order out loud once without notes, then add おいしいです (oishii desu, it is tasty)

plans.goal: Greet someone, exchange names and say thank you in Telugu.

tasks: Learn నమస్కారం (namaskāraṁ, hello) and బాగున్నారా? (bāgunnārā?, are you well?). Say them out loud ten times
Learn బాగున్నాను (bāgunnānu, I am well)
Watch Daily Telugu 01 and repeat after the teacher
Learn మీ పేరు ఏమిటి? (mī pēru ēmiṭi?, what is your name?) and నా పేరు 〇〇 (nā pēru 〇〇, my name is 〇〇)
Role-play a first meeting with Claude
Learn ధన్యవాదాలు (dhanyavādālu, thank you) and run the whole greeting once without notes
